title: House gives preliminary approval to $70.8 billion spending plan
summary: The House is poised to give final approval to a $70.8 billion operating budget package for fiscal 2027 as early as Thursday, setting up the possibility a final deal could be reached with the Senate and a budget delivered to the governor before the end of the session.
content:
by Bryan P. Sears, Maryland Matters March 26, 2026

by Bryan P. Sears, Maryland Matters March 26, 2026

The House is poised to give final approval to a $70.8 billion operating budget package for fiscal 2027 as early as Thursday.

The vote, with less than three weeks left in the 90-day legislative session, sets up an atypical scenario where the final budget could be delivered to Gov. Wes Moore for approval before the end of the session.

“There’s a lot to be proud of in this budget,” said House Appropriations Chair Ben Barnes (D-Anne Arundel and Prince George’s County).

As with the Senate version, which won final approval last week, the House version closes a $1.5 billion shortfall with no tax or fee increases.

The budget as presented to the House leaves a cash surplus for the coming year of $280 million. That is in addition to more than $2 billion in the state’s rainy day fund. It’s an amount equal to about 8% of general fund revenues.

And while House Democrats noted the package includes support for state employees, many of those employees will receive raises that do not keep up with inflation.

House Republicans offered more than a dozen amendments across the two-bill budget package this week.

One amendment, to require nonprofits be up-to-date with their mandated reporting to the state before receiving state grants, was passed.

House Minority Leader Del. Jason C. Buckel (R-Allegany), said his amendment would establish guardrails for the state when it provides grant funding to nonprofits.

Buckel said the amendment “would increase transparency and make sure that if you’re taking government money to provide a charitable purpose, you’re doing it in the right way, you’re certified and you’re up to date with everything that we require of you.”

A similar amendment was offered in the Senate and rejected.

“I do think this amendment reflects the mandate from our speaker this year on accountability,” Barnes said in support of the amendment. “I think it supports the work done by GLE and by the Joint Audits Committee and the great work that they’ve done, and also work by the budget committee on budget language to make sure we’re doing as much accountability as possible with that. I think this does help that process.”

More than a dozen amendments to the budget reconciliation bill were offered by Republicans. The vast majority focused on taxes and fees.

House Minority Whip Jesse T. Pippy (R-Frederick) told reporters before the vote that Republicans developed a list of “400 plus” increases of taxes or fees.

“It’s outrageous. And so we’re going to follow through on what we pledged at the beginning of session, which is we want to make Maryland more affordable,” Pippy said. “And so today’s the day. It’s Maryland Day. The Republican Caucus is going to do everything we can to make Maryland affordable today, and we hope that the majority party will work with us on this issue.”

Included on the GOP hit list were the sales tax approved last year on information technology and data services, fees for vehicle registrations and emissions testing, and some fishing licenses fees.

One by one those amendments were rejected.

YOU MAKE OUR WORK POSSIBLE.

The House also rejected an amendment offered by Del. Todd Morgan (R-Calvert and St. Mary’s) to impose a 30-day holiday on the 46-cent per gallon state gas tax.

A final vote by the House would set up a conference committee with the Senate Friday. Lawmakers in both chambers said the differences between the House and Senate versions are small and a conference should be brief. The conference committee is expected to incorporate a second supplemental budget request from Gov. Wes Moore (D).

Details of that request are not fully known. It is expected to account for updated revenue projections issued earlier this month by the Board of Revenue Estimates.

For the second consecutive year, the House has snatched away a modest victory by Senate Republicans.

The House Appropriations committee struck a Senate Republican amendment on when a vehicle is eligible for historic plates. The current law sets the date of the car at 1999 or earlier. The Senate amendment changed it to any vehicle that is at least 25 years old.

Del. Chris Tomlinson (R-Frederick and Carroll) offered an amendment to restore the provision in the House. Again, the Democratic supermajority rejected it.

The House version also limits participation in the governor’s service-year program to 750 young adults.
